newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: OPPOSITION SAYS GOVT MOVE ON COLSTON VOTES INADEQUATE
The Federal Opposition says the Prime Minister's offer to cancel out any vote by Indepdenent Senator Mal Colston, doesn't go far enough.
The government has decided it will act to neutralise any attempt by Senator Colston to vote with the Coalition.
Senator Colston is under investigation by the Federal Police over allegations of travel rorts, and is under pressure to stand down as senate Deputy President.
A spokesman for Opposition Leader Kim Beazley says the offer is fine, but it's only part of a piecemeal approach by the Government to the issue.
The spokesman says Mal Colston should go, and Mr Howard should ensure that happens.
HOWARD SAYS WIK AGREEMENT DIFFICULT
The Prime Minister, John Howard, says obsession with a timetable for the Government's response to the High Court's Wik decision on native title is not helpful.
Mr Howard briefed Cabinet at length yesterday on options for a response, and will spend the week in further negotiations with stakeholders.
Mr Howard has told the ABC time is required to reach a fair accommodation, and the right decision is more important than whether it's today, tomorrow or next week.
He says he hasn't got an agreed position yet and believes it will be very difficult.
WALLIS STANDS BY CLAIMS BANK CHARGES WILL DROP

The author of the report on Australia's financial system, Stan Wallis, says he's sure there'll be lower charges for customers using new banking systems, even though one bank has just increased it's fees.

The Colonial State Bank has doubled charges on savings and deposit accounts, and introduced a charge on EFTPOS purchases. The move came days after the Wallis report recommended banks be free to set their fees and charges, and that electronic banking be developed further.
Mr Wallis says he has no doubt there are savings to be made by encouraging the new modes of banking and the Colonial Bank's move is an individual institution's decision.
MILLIONS OF DOLLARS IN CASH SEIZED FROM BOAT
More than five million dollars in cash has been seized by Federal Police and Customs Officers, in a raid on a commercial vessel at Port Alma, in Central Queensland.
The vessel, the Neptune Wind, was raided earlier this month.
Five meat cartons on the boat, contained five-million-one-hundred and 25 thousand dollars .
The find was the result of an investigation into large-scale importation of cannabis.
A number of people in Queensland and New South Wales have been charged with offences, under the Crimes, Customs, Migration, and Proceeds of Crimes Acts.
WALLIS CRITICISES CONSUMER WATCHDOG
The head of the inquiry into the Australian Financial System, Stan Wallis, has criticised the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, which he says has gone after the high profile cases.
The Wallis report, released last week, recommends the Commission's consumer protection role be taken over by a new authority.
Mr Wallis has told ABC radio that while the A-triple-C has achieved some success, the high profile cases are only the top end consumer protection issues.
He says there's a need for a focussed regulator who can do the job properly.
ACCC Chairman, Alan Fels, rejects the criticism, saying the Commission has never lacked resources to pursue cases.
EMPLOYER ACCESS TO PAEDOPHILE DATABASE PROPOSED
Police will tell employers of the presence of convicted and suspected child sex offenders in their organisation, if Federal Crime agencies have their way.
The Australian Bureau of Criminal Intelligence will present a plan for such an iniative to Australiasian Police Ministers when they meet in July.

The Australian Bureau of Criminal Intelligence says barriers which prevent the release of information on suspects to third parties must be removed if a national database on paedophiles is to protect children.
The matter was raised at a conference on paedophilia in Sydney.
It was told that as part of the initiative, a national body would be established to screen child sex offenders from employment in which they are likely to interact with children.
MARK TAYLOR SAYS HE WON'T STAND DOWN

Australian Test Cricket Captain Mark Taylor says the Australian selectors have told him not to stand down from the position, and he hasn't heard from the Australian Cricket board telling him to do so.
There's been speculation about Taylor's future following his poor form on the recent tour to South Africa.
The 17-man Australian squad arrived home today, having won both the test and one-day series.
Taylor says at the moment he's not standing down and he hopes to captain the Australian side to England for the ashes tour begining next month.
